title: 3D Home Building
desc: Understand how large-scale 3D printing of walls and homes works, its safety, codes, costs and where it suits.
outcomes: Explain how a construction printer builds walls.
Write a feasibility note for a small building.
task: Write a feasibility note for a small printed building with design, quantities, time, cost, code checks and risks.
condition: A computer, public information, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor builder. No printer operation is done.
standard: Quantities and time are calculated; code and permit checks are listed; risks and controls are stated; cost compared with conventional building; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Builders, architects in training, housing groups, students.
evidence: quantity sheet, cost comparison, risk list, note
modules: A construction 3D printer builds walls by laying a cement-like mix in layers, following a digital path.
A gantry or robotic arm moves a nozzle over the site.
Walls are printed in layers of 15 to 40 mm; doors, windows, roof and services are added by trades.
A design file controls the path; changing the file changes the building.
Printing is fast for walls but the whole building still needs foundations, roof and finishes.
A printer lays a 40 mm bead in a double-wall pattern with hollow cavities, which are later filled with reinforcement and insulation.
Draw the process from design file to finished wall with labels.
All steps are shown in order.
Cement-based mixes with additives, earth mixes and recycled aggregates.
The mix must flow through the nozzle, hold shape and gain strength.
Weather affects curing; heat and wind dry layers quickly.
On a hot day a retarder is added so layers bond before drying.
Compare two mixes in a table.
Printed buildings follow the same safety codes as others.
Structural design by a qualified engineer, including reinforcement and openings.
Fire, energy, accessibility and ventilation codes.
Steel bars are placed in wall cavities before they are filled, and an engineer signs the design.
List code checks for a small building in your place.
Wall length x height / layer height = layers.
60 m of wall at 3 m high with 20 mm layers needs 150 layers.
People and machines share the site.
Exclusion zones, emergency stop and lifting plans.
A fence marks the print zone and a trained operator stays on watch.
Labour saving vs machine and material cost.
Walls cost 12 per cent less but doors and roofing cost the same.
A cube fails the strength test and the batch is rejected.
The note recommends a small pilot hut before a house.

ladder: How it works

L1: learner can describe printing. Focus module: How it works (Understand, 3 h). Layers of material. Key points: A gantry or arm prints a cement-like mix in layers. Walls are printed; roofs and services are added by hand. A design file controls the path.

Teach: open with the worked example. A printer lays a 40 mm bead in a double-wall pattern. Then set the activity: Draw the process. Mark against the standard: Steps labelled. Check at this level: How is a wall built? Model answer: In layers by a gantry or arm. Process.
Materials

L2: learner knows materials. Focus module: Materials (Understand, 3 h). The mix decides success. Key points: Cement mixes with additives; earth mixes; recycled aggregates. Must flow, hold shape and cure. Weather affects curing.

Teach: open with the worked example. A hot day needs a retarder. Then set the activity: Compare two mixes. Mark against the standard: Properties listed. Check at this level: What controls the path? Model answer: A design file. Mix.
Design and codes

L3: learner can read codes. Focus module: Design and codes (Apply, 4 h). Printing is not exempt. Key points: Structural design by an engineer; reinforcement and openings. Fire, energy and accessibility codes. Foundations and utilities as usual.

Teach: open with the worked example. Steel bars are placed in wall cavities. Then set the activity: List code checks. Mark against the standard: Sources noted. Check at this level: Who designs structure? Model answer: An engineer. Codes.
Quantities and time

L4: learner can count. Focus module: Quantities and time (Analyse, 4 h). Count the bead. Key points: Wall length x height / layer height = layers. Volume x density = material. Print speed gives hours.

Teach: open with the worked example. 60 m of wall at 3 m high needs 150 layers of 20 mm. Then set the activity: Calculate for a small room. Mark against the standard: Maths correct. Check at this level: Layers formula? Model answer: Height / layer height. Sums.
Site and safety
L5: learner can compare cost. Focus module: Site and safety (Evaluate, 4 h). People and machine. Key points: Exclusion zones, emergency stop, lifting. Dust and silica protection. Weather plan.

Teach: open with the worked example. A fence marks the print zone. Then set the activity: Write a site safety plan. Mark against the standard: Plan approved by mentor. Check at this level: Silica danger? Model answer: Dust harms lungs. Costs.
Quality control
L6: learner can lead a crew. Focus module: Quality control (Apply, 3 h). Test it. Key points: Sample cubes for strength. Check layer bonding and tolerances. Keep records.

Teach: open with the worked example. A cube fails; the batch is rejected. Then set the activity: Write a QC plan. Mark against the standard: Tests named. Check at this level: Why cube tests? Model answer: Check strength. Lead.
Feasibility note
L7: learner can audit. Focus module: Feasibility note (Create, 4 h). Pull it together. Key points: Fit: housing, shelters, small buildings. Risks and permits. Next steps.

Teach: open with the worked example. The note recommends a small pilot hut. Then set the activity: Write and present. Mark against the standard: Reader can decide. Check at this level: What stays manual? Model answer: Roof and services. Peer audit.
